errors.english: since it is distinct from the probandum [note: the thesis to be proven] such as the possessor of connection
errors.why: The Tibetan says the probandum is distinct from the saṃyogin etc.; the English makes the saṃyogin an example of the probandum.

note: A sound rendering of a dense Pramāṇa passage on tadātmya/tadutpatti versus saṃyoga, with one mis-segmented clause in the objection.

errors.english: pervaded by one part of the side of the property of the property-bearer to be proved
errors.why: The formula is 'a property of the dharmin to be proved (pakṣadharma), pervaded by a part of the pakṣa'; the English nests the genitives wrongly and renders pakṣa as 'side'.

note: Careful and accurate on the pervasion analysis and the three restrictions; only the opening citation of the hetu formula is garbled.

errors.english: Regarding that which relates to the essential nature of the (dharmin) subject
errors.why: In this list of pakṣābhāsas (cf. the previous side's ཆོས་ཀྱི་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་དང་འགལ་བ) འབྲེལ་བ is a corruption for འགལ་བ: 'contradiction of the dharmin's own nature' (dharmisvarūpa-viruddha), not 'that which relates to' it.

note: Good translation of the discussion of svayam and iṣṭa in the thesis definition; it follows one corrupt reading that a specialist would emend.
Faithful rendering of the argument against qualifying sādharmya, with the verse lines correctly set off.

errors.english: introduces the Sankhya [note: one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy] position, namely, "color and so forth."
errors.why: Here གྲངས་ཅན means the enumerated items that 'and so forth' introduces (namely colour etc.), not the Sāṃkhya school; the note compounds the error.

errors.english: However many there are, and which are also excluded, is in reference to seeing them.
errors.why: བསལ་བ is a slip for གསལ་བ (individual, vyakti), as the next side shows: 'seeing however many there are that are individuals', not 'excluded'.

note: The objection-and-reply structure of the apoha passage is followed well, but two terms are misread and the Sāṃkhya note will mislead.

errors.english: motivated solely by compassion for worldly beings
errors.why: PV kevalaṃ lokabuddhyaiva: 'solely by the world's understanding', as the commentary's 'in accordance with the world's clinging appearance' confirms; 'compassion' is not in the text.

fix.find: motivated solely by compassion for worldly beings
fix.replace: solely in accordance with the understanding of the world

errors.english: [note: Tibetan: (glang chen gzigs stangs), Sanskrit: (nāgāvalokita), referring to the solemn, direct gaze of a Buddha turning the whole body]
errors.why: In PV III this is gajanimīlana, the elephant's feigned not-seeing, as the commentary itself glosses ('though seeing, they show as if not seeing'); the nāgāvalokita note is wrong.

fix.find: [note: Tibetan: (glang chen gzigs stangs), Sanskrit: (nāgāvalokita), referring to the solemn, direct gaze of a Buddha turning the whole body]
fix.replace: [note: Tibetan: (glang chen gzigs stangs), Sanskrit: (gajanimīlana), the elephant's feigned not-seeing: seeing, yet acting as though one did not see]

errors.english: who possess equanimity toward the meaning of reality
errors.why: upekṣya tattvārtham: the Buddhas set aside or disregard the ultimate meaning when teaching, rather than having 'equanimity' toward it.

errors.english: If one asks: who are those who are not endowed with the nature of reality
errors.why: The verse says 'this is not suited to reality — for whom? for all who do not see the highest'; the English turns the predicate into a question about persons lacking reality.

note: The Yogācāra argument is followed, but the closing PV verse on the Buddhas' worldly teaching is mistranslated and mis-glossed.

errors.english: For if that transformation were without a cause
errors.why: དེ refers to the distinction in consciousness, which would be causeless if there were no distinction in the transformation, not to the transformation itself.

note: A sound translation of the anti-materialist milk analogy, with one referent misidentified.

errors.english: because there is no intention, and because it is not the proper basis, there is no infraction in any of these cases for one who acts without a deceitful mind
errors.why: The Tibetan says 'without supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) it is not a field' and 'for one with a mind of disbelief'; neither 'no intention' nor 'without a deceitful mind' is there.

errors.english: However, if the carrier positioned on land within the border does have a need, it constitutes a grave offense.
errors.why: The rule is: where the mantra/medicine power does not require the carrier to stand on ground within the boundary there is no offense, while a carrier standing within the boundary incurs a sthūlātyaya; the English makes it turn on whether the carrier 'has a need'.

note: The Vinaya rulings on customs evasion through the air are mostly right, but the final cases on miraculous and mantra-borne transport are misconstrued.

errors.english: And it is not so: if it had parts, it would not exist as a real substance.
errors.why: Here དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ means 'otherwise', introducing the reason why it must be partless; 'And it is not so' reads as a denial of the preceding claim.

note: An accurate rendering of the argument that shape differences belong only to conventional, part-possessing things.

errors.english: The actions of the Supreme Sage
errors.why: MMK 17.2 (karmoktaṃ paramarṣiṇā): actions in general were taught by the Supreme Sage to be cetanā and cetayitvā; they are not the Buddha's own actions.

fix.find: The actions of the Supreme Sage

errors.english: It should be understood how these are produced.
errors.why: This finishes the previous side's sentence: the neutral (avyākṛta) items should be understood to produce a cause-concordant result, not 'how these are produced'.

note: Generally faithful on the cetanā/cetayitvā division, but the root verse makes the Buddha the owner of the actions instead of their teacher.
